post.description:
End one admitted run early and release its team's concurrency slot.

The body is read by hand rather than declared as a parameter so that the token check
runs **first**. FastAPI resolves a declared body during dependency solving, which
would answer a malformed anonymous request with a validation error — telling an
unauthenticated caller the shape of an organizer-only surface. The scoring ingest
endpoint reads its body the same way, for the same reason.

get.description: The public leaderboard, best run first. No session required.

post.description:
Post a scored run. Called by the scoring pass the moment aggregation completes.

Query parameters, all optional:

- ``replace`` — overwrite the row this run already has. Without it a run already on
  the board is refused with ``409`` rather than silently overwritten: correcting a row
  is legitimate and an accidental second post is not, and before #122 the two were
  indistinguishable at this boundary.
- ``dry_run`` — parse and check the payload, post nothing, and report what a real post
  would do. This is the "validate it before it is public" step, run by the server that
  would publish it rather than by a second copy of its rules.
- ``allow_ended`` — post a run an organizer ended early (#122). Off by default.

Who is posting rides in the ``X-JPC-Performed-By`` header rather than the query
string, because the query string is what lands in every access and proxy log along the
path and an organizer's name is not something to scatter there.

**Nothing is parsed before the token is checked.** Neither the query string nor the
body is declared as a parameter, because FastAPI resolves a declared parameter during
dependency solving — before this function runs — and would answer an anonymous caller
with a validation error describing an organizer-only surface. `queue/internal.py`
reads its body by hand for the same reason and cites this endpoint as the precedent;
it is the precedent only if it actually does it.

post.description:
Check a submission, and — when the team asked for it — queue it.

Both buttons post here. ``check`` runs validation and stops; ``submit`` runs the same
validation and only then asks the queue for a slot, so a rejected submission leaves the
team's queue state exactly as it found it.

A third outcome since #110: a second copy of a form already acted on is refused before
either. This is the page the issue was filed about — two concurrent posts spent two of a
team's three queue slots for one intended submission — but the guard is the shared one,
so ``check`` is covered by the same rule as ``submit`` and neither page has a rule of its
own to keep in step.

BreakdownRow.title: BreakdownRow
BreakdownRow.description:
Token usage for one ``(agent, task, wave, model)`` combination, summed over items.

Aggregated across items on purpose: a per-item row would carry item identity into the
one view that is available while a hidden run is still in flight.

CapsView.title: CapsView
CapsView.description:
The caps this run executed under, as its own record captured them.

Shown beside the capped-item counts, because `capped_tokens` is an opaque state until
the number beside it turns it into "you spent the run's token budget".

DevKeyListResponse.description: The team's keys plus the cap they count against.

DiagnosisView.title: DiagnosisView
DiagnosisView.description:
The run-level answer to "what went wrong, and whose problem is it?".

This is what a team with forty failed items actually needs: the summary, said once.
The per-item table below it is the drill-down, and it is a different field behind a
different gate.

EndRunResponse.title: EndRunResponse
EndRunResponse.description: What ending the run did, or would do.

FailureGroupView.title: FailureGroupView
FailureGroupView.description:
How many items failed for one reason, and whose problem that reason is.

A count, never a list. There is deliberately no item id on this shape and
``extra="forbid"`` refuses one, which is what makes the group safe to render while a
hidden run is in flight.

FailureKind.title: FailureKind
FailureKind.description:
Why an LLM call or an item failed.

The evaluation endpoint is intermittently unavailable -- five independent outages
were observed in one afternoon (`runner/SPIKE-REPORT.md` finding 9). Without this
field an outage is indistinguishable from a squad that answered badly, and AI:GO's
failure-as-context semantics turn an unretried connect timeout into "execution
completed, all tasks failed", which grading would read as a team's zero.

`ItemStatus` already keeps an outage out of the cap and out of a graded answer:
`ERROR` is neither `CAPPED_*` nor `OK`, and the extractor maps it to
`Outcome.EXTRACTION_FAILED`, never a silent zero. This field says *whose* fault the
error was, which is what decides whether the item is re-run or the team is told.

FailureOwner.title: FailureOwner
FailureOwner.description:
Whose problem a failure is: the column `docs/contracts/run-record.md` publishes.

The ownership column of that table is a fact about the vocabulary, not about any one
surface's presentation of it, which is why it lives here rather than in a renderer.
Two consumers already need it and were deriving it separately: grading excludes
judge-owned outcomes from a ranked denominator (`score.py`, issue #54), and the
team-facing run pages have to say whether a failed item is the team's problem or the
organizer's (issue #86). A second derivation is a second chance to get it wrong.

A healthy item has no `FailureKind` at all; its outcome belongs to :attr:`TEAM`, which
is why that member exists here without a kind mapping to it.

ItemOutcomeView.description:
One item's identity, execution status and failure classification.

Built only once the guard allows item identities, which is what keeps the per-item
drill-down off a hidden run in flight while the per-kind summary still renders.

LeaderboardEntryResponse.title: LeaderboardEntryResponse
LeaderboardEntryResponse.description: One posted run, with its place on the board.

caps_note.title: Caps Note
caps_note.default: Comparability: every run on this page executed under a per-item wall-clock cap and a per-run token cap, identical for every team. Runs that executed under different caps are not directly comparable, and the difference is not a small correction. Two of the three evaluation models are reasoning models — one was measured spending 97% of its output budget on reasoning tokens before it answered — so a token cap bites roughly an order of magnitude harder on a squad built from reasoning models than on one built from an instruct model. Read the caps column before comparing two rows.

LeaderboardResponse.title: LeaderboardResponse
LeaderboardResponse.description:
The board, plus every notice the page is obliged to carry.

The HTML page and this response are built from the same
:func:`~jpc_server.leaderboard.rendering.build_view` output, so a field is added here
when the page starts showing something a machine reader could not otherwise derive —
additively, and never as a second projection of the same rows.

What is deliberately *not* here: the spectator guide. The lede, the track descriptions
and the how-to-read entries are constant contest description with no per-run content,
and an API client that wanted them would be reading documentation, not data.

ModelTokens.title: ModelTokens
ModelTokens.description:
Token usage attributed to one model id, straight from ``RunRecord.model_usage``.

Per *model*, never per agent: the finer per-agent/per-task breakdown stays on the
team's private run-details page (plan §6).

ModelUsageView.title: ModelUsageView
ModelUsageView.description: Per-model token usage, straight off the run record's own aggregate.

Outcome.title: Outcome
Outcome.description:
Why an item scored what it scored.

`EXTRACTION_FAILED` is distinct from a graded-wrong answer on purpose: a silent
zero hides a harness defect behind a team's score (issue #12).

Two of the five are **judge-owned**: `GRADER_ERROR` and `INFRASTRUCTURE_FAILED`. Nothing
a squad's output can do causes either one, so neither is priced into a ranked
denominator -- see `docs/contracts/grading.md` §4.2. The other three are the team's
outcome, whether or not the team likes it.

OutcomeCountView.title: OutcomeCountView
OutcomeCountView.description:
How many of a track's items reached one grading outcome.

A count per outcome and nothing else: no item id, no grader evidence, no answer. That
is what lets extraction failure be shown as its own thing without reopening anything
``sanitize`` closed.

ProgressView.title: ProgressView
ProgressView.description: Counts, and only counts. Safe for a hidden run in flight.

PublicItemLine.title: PublicItemLine
PublicItemLine.description:
One item a run was scored on, in the only shape a public page may show it.

Emitted exclusively for items whose disclosure level is ``public``. Everything else
contributes to the counts on its track row and to nothing else — see
:func:`jpc_server.leaderboard.composition.compose_publication`.

PublicationAccepted.title: PublicationAccepted
PublicationAccepted.description:
Acknowledgement that a scored run was posted — or, under a dry run, was not.

The three added fields are what makes re-publication *visible* rather than incidental.
Updating a row instead of duplicating it has always been the behaviour (#19), and it
is right; what was missing is the caller being told which of the two things just
happened to the event's public record.

PublishedCaps.title: PublishedCaps
PublishedCaps.description:
The caps one run *executed under*, as that run's own record reported them.

Not :class:`jpc_server.queue.policy.RunCaps`. That model is the queue's **input**
policy — what a run is launched with, every field required and positive. This is a
**report** of what a run actually ran under, and a report is whatever the runner wrote:
a cap that was not in force is ``null``, and the block carries ``infra_retries``, which
is not a cap the queue sets at all. Validating the report against the policy is what
made the caps footnote read ``not recorded`` on every real record (#108); the two are
separate types now so that it cannot happen again by resemblance.

The numbers are read by :meth:`jpc_server.status.snapshot.CapsSnapshot.of`, the same
reader the team-facing run pages use, so the two surfaces cannot come to disagree about
what a runner writes. ``docs/contracts/leaderboard.md`` states the relationship.

Four states, and the page prints a different thing for each:

- ``recorded=False, readable=True`` — the record carried no caps block. Nothing is
  known, and this is the only state that may print ``not recorded``.
- ``readable=False`` — a caps block was there and could not be read. That is a defect
  in this reader or a shape change in the runner, and it must never be able to pass
  for the state above, because that is precisely how #108 stayed invisible.
- ``recorded=True`` with a ``None`` cap — the block was there and that cap was not in
  force. A real record writes ``per_run_token_cap: null`` exactly this way.
- ``recorded=True`` with a number — that cap was in force, at that value.
